claim: Cilia are complex evolutionarily conserved eukaryotic structures composed of hundreds of proteins required for their assembly, structure and function that are collectively known as the ciliome.
source: Cilia, either motile or non-motile (a.k.a primary or sensory), are complex evolutionarily conserved eukaryotic structures composed of hundreds of proteins required for their assembly, structure and function that are collectively known as the ciliome.
evidence: This is a definitional statement about cilia and the ciliome that draws from established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: Ciliome gene mutations underlie a group of pleiotropic genetic diseases known as ciliopathies.
source: Ciliome gene mutations underlie a group of pleiotropic genetic diseases known as ciliopathies.
evidence: This statement reflects established scientific knowledge about the relationship between ciliome gene mutations and ciliopathies.

claim: RFX transcription factors have an evolutionarily conserved role in the direct activation of ciliome genes both in motile and non-motile cilia cell-types.
source: RFX transcription factors (TF) have an evolutionarily conserved role in the direct activation of ciliome genes both in motile and non-motile cilia cell-types.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research establishing RFX function across organisms.

claim: In vertebrates, FoxJ1 and FoxN4 Forkhead TFs work with RFX in the direct activation of ciliome genes, exclusively in motile cilia cell-types.
source: In vertebrates, FoxJ1 and FoxN4 Forkhead (FKH) TFs work with RFX in the direct activation of ciliome genes, exclusively in motile cilia cell-types.
evidence: This statement is supported by prior research on vertebrate FoxJ1 and FoxN4 function in motile cilia.

claim: No additional TFs have been described to act together with RFX in primary cilia cell-types in any organism prior to this study.
source: No additional TFs have been described to act together with RFX in primary cilia cell-types in any organism.
evidence: This statement reflects the state of knowledge in the field prior to the current study.

claim: FKH-8 is a FKH TF that acts as a direct regulator of sensory ciliome genes in Caenorhabditis elegans.
source: Here we describe FKH-8, a FKH TF, as a direct regulator of the sensory ciliome genes in Caenorhabditis elegans.
evidence: This is the main finding of the manuscript, supported by multiple experimental approaches including ChIP-seq, mutant analysis, and reporter assays.

claim: FKH-8 is expressed in all ciliated neurons in C. elegans.
source: FKH-8 is expressed in all ciliated neurons in C. elegans, binds the regulatory regions of ciliome genes, regulates ciliome gene expression, cilium morphology and a wide range of behaviors mediated by sensory ciliated neurons.
evidence: This is supported by fosmid reporter expression data and sc-RNA-seq analysis shown in the manuscript.

claim: FKH-8 binds the regulatory regions of ciliome genes.
source: FKH-8 is expressed in all ciliated neurons in C. elegans, binds the regulatory regions of ciliome genes, regulates ciliome gene expression, cilium morphology and a wide range of behaviors mediated by sensory ciliated neurons.
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-seq data analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: FKH-8 regulates ciliome gene expression.
source: FKH-8 is expressed in all ciliated neurons in C. elegans, binds the regulatory regions of ciliome genes, regulates ciliome gene expression, cilium morphology and a wide range of behaviors mediated by sensory ciliated neurons.
evidence: This is supported by reporter expression analysis in fkh-8 mutants and endogenous gene expression measurements.

claim: FKH-8 regulates cilium morphology.
source: FKH-8 is expressed in all ciliated neurons in C. elegans, binds the regulatory regions of ciliome genes, regulates ciliome gene expression, cilium morphology and a wide range of behaviors mediated by sensory ciliated neurons.
evidence: This is supported by cilium length and morphology measurements in fkh-8 mutants.

claim: FKH-8 regulates a wide range of behaviors mediated by sensory ciliated neurons.
source: FKH-8 is expressed in all ciliated neurons in C. elegans, binds the regulatory regions of ciliome genes, regulates ciliome gene expression, cilium morphology and a wide range of behaviors mediated by sensory ciliated neurons.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral assays showing defects in multiple sensory modalities in fkh-8 mutants.

claim: FKH-8 and DAF-19 physically interact.
source: FKH-8 and DAF-19 (C. elegans RFX) physically interact and synergistically regulate ciliome gene expression.
evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation experiments in HEK293 cells.

claim: FKH-8 and DAF-19 synergistically regulate ciliome gene expression.
source: FKH-8 and DAF-19 (C. elegans RFX) physically interact and synergistically regulate ciliome gene expression.
evidence: This is supported by double mutant analysis showing greater than multiplicative effects on reporter expression.

claim: C. elegans FKH-8 function can be replaced by mouse FOXJ1.
source: C. elegans FKH-8 function can be replaced by mouse FOXJ1 and FOXN4 but not by other members of other mouse FKH subfamilies.
evidence: This is supported by rescue experiments showing mouse FOXJ1 can restore ift-20 expression in fkh-8 mutants.

claim: C. elegans FKH-8 function can be replaced by mouse FOXN4.
source: C. elegans FKH-8 function can be replaced by mouse FOXJ1 and FOXN4 but not by other members of other mouse FKH subfamilies.
evidence: This is supported by rescue experiments showing mouse FOXN4 can restore ift-20 expression in fkh-8 mutants.

claim: C. elegans FKH-8 function cannot be replaced by other members of mouse FKH subfamilies.
source: C. elegans FKH-8 function can be replaced by mouse FOXJ1 and FOXN4 but not by other members of other mouse FKH subfamilies.
evidence: This is supported by rescue experiments showing mouse FOXI1 cannot restore ift-20 expression in fkh-8 mutants.

claim: RFX and FKH TF families act jointly as direct regulators of ciliome genes in sensory ciliated cell types.
source: In conclusion, RFX and FKH TF families act jointly as direct regulators of ciliome genes also in sensory ciliated cell types suggesting that this regulatory logic could be an ancient trait predating functional cilia sub-specialization.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the experimental data presented in the manuscript showing FKH-8 and DAF-19 cooperation.

claim: The regulatory logic of RFX and FKH TFs acting together could be an ancient trait predating functional cilia sub-specialization.
source: In conclusion, RFX and FKH TF families act jointly as direct regulators of ciliome genes also in sensory ciliated cell types suggesting that this regulatory logic could be an ancient trait predating functional cilia sub-specialization.
evidence: This is a speculative evolutionary interpretation based on the conservation of function between C. elegans FKH-8 and vertebrate FOXJ1/FOXN4.

claim: Motile cilia are responsible for propelling cells or generating fluid flow.
source: Cilia can be classified into motile or non-motile based on their function and structure: motile cilia are responsible for propelling cells or generating fluid flow while non-motile (a.k.a primary or sensory) cilia function as cellular antennae to sense extracellular stimuli (Choksi et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge about cilia function, supported by citation.

claim: Non-motile cilia function as cellular antennae to sense extracellular stimuli.
source: Cilia can be classified into motile or non-motile based on their function and structure: motile cilia are responsible for propelling cells or generating fluid flow while non-motile (a.k.a primary or sensory) cilia function as cellular antennae to sense extracellular stimuli (Choksi et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge about cilia function, supported by citation.

claim: In ancient unicellular eukaryotes cilia displayed mixed motile and sensory functions.
source: Cilia appeared early in eukaryotic evolution and it is thought that in ancient unicellular eukaryotes cilia displayed mixed motile and sensory functions (Mitchell, 2017).
evidence: This is a hypothesis about ancestral cilia function supported by citation.

claim: In multicellular invertebrates, primary and motor cilia are restricted to specific cell types.
source: In multicellular invertebrates, primary and motor cilia are restricted to specific cell types.
evidence: This is established knowledge about cilia distribution in invertebrates.

claim: In vertebrates, primary cilia are present almost in every cell, including neurons.
source: In contrast, in vertebrates, primary cilia are present almost in every cell, including neurons, while motile cilia are present only in specialized cell types.
evidence: This is established knowledge about cilia distribution in vertebrates.

claim: In vertebrates, motile cilia are present only in specialized cell types.
source: In contrast, in vertebrates, primary cilia are present almost in every cell, including neurons, while motile cilia are present only in specialized cell types.
evidence: This is established knowledge about cilia distribution in vertebrates.

claim: FKH-8::GFP fosmid expression at young adult stage is detected in all ciliated sensory neurons.
source: FKH-8::GFP fosmid expression at young adult stage is detected in all ciliated sensory neurons, as assessed by co-localization with the ift-20 core ciliome reporter (Figure 2A and B and Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data showing co-localization with ift-20 reporter.

claim: Three non-ciliated neurons, PVD, VC4 and VC5 show FKH-8 expression.
source: Three non-ciliated neurons, PVD, VC4 and VC5 show FKH-8 expression, while no expression is detected in non-neuronal tissues.
evidence: This is based on observation of FKH-8::GFP reporter expression.

claim: No FKH-8 expression is detected in non-neuronal tissues.
source: Three non-ciliated neurons, PVD, VC4 and VC5 show FKH-8 expression, while no expression is detected in non-neuronal tissues.
evidence: This is based on observation of FKH-8::GFP reporter expression.

claim: C. elegans male nervous system contains additional ciliated sensory neurons, mostly in the tail, which also express FKH-8.
source: C. elegans male nervous system contains additional ciliated sensory neurons, mostly in the tail, which also express FKH-8 (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data of FKH-8::GFP expression in males.

claim: During embryonic development, there is overlap between FKH-8 and ift-20 reporters.
source: During embryonic development, there is a similar overlap between FKH-8 and ift-20 reporters (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by embryonic expression analysis shown in supplementary figures.

claim: There is correlation between fkh-8, ift-20 and daf-19 expression during development using UMAP representation of embryonic sc-RNA-seq data.
source: Correlation between fkh-8, ift-20 and daf-19 expression during development is also observed using Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection (UMAP) representation of embryonic sc-RNA-seq data (Packer et al., 2019; Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of published sc-RNA-seq data.

claim: There is high gene expression correlation for the 73 core ciliome genes and daf-19 or fkh-8 expression but not with other TFs.
source: In addition, there is a high gene expression correlation for the 73 core ciliome genes and daf-19 or fkh-8 expression but not with other TFs (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis of sc-RNA-seq data.

claim: FKH-8 is expressed almost exclusively in the whole ciliated sensory system.
source: Thus, our analysis shows that FKH-8 is expressed almost exclusively in the whole ciliated sensory system and its developmental expression correlates with core ciliome gene expression.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the expression data presented.

claim: FKH-8 developmental expression correlates with core ciliome gene expression.
source: Thus, our analysis shows that FKH-8 is expressed almost exclusively in the whole ciliated sensory system and its developmental expression correlates with core ciliome gene expression.
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis of expression data.

claim: Genes associated to nearby FKH-8 binding events enrich Gene Ontology terms related to cilia regulated processes and/or functions.
source: Gene ontology analysis of FKH-8 bound genes shows enrichment for cilia functions or dauer regulation (which is also dependent on cilia integrity; Figure 2C, Figure 2—source data 2).
evidence: This is supported by Gene Ontology analysis of ChIP-seq data.

claim: De novo motif analysis of FKH-8 ChIP-seq data identifies a motif present in 27% of peaks that matches a Forkhead like (FHL) motif.
source: De novo motif enrichment analysis of FKH-8 ChIP-seq peaks does not show any match for FKH canonical binding site but identifies a motif that highly resembles the FHL motif (Figure 2D). This motif, present in 27% of the peaks, is enriched at central positions suggesting it could act as FKH-8 primary binding motif (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by computational motif analysis of ChIP-seq peaks.

claim: The FHL motif identified in FKH-8 ChIP-seq peaks is enriched at central positions.
source: This motif, present in 27% of the peaks, is enriched at central positions suggesting it could act as FKH-8 primary binding motif (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by positional analysis of motif occurrences in ChIP-seq peaks.

claim: Eight out of the 12 functional X-boxes present in the core ciliome gene reporters overlap with FKH-8 ChIP-seq peaks.
source: We noticed that eight out of the 12 functional X-boxes present in the core ciliome gene reporters analyzed in Figure 1C overlap with FKH-8 ChIP-seq peaks (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on comparison of known X-box locations with ChIP-seq peak locations.

claim: 21% of FKH-8 peaks contain at least one match for the DAF-19 position weight matrix.
source: 21% of FKH-8 peaks contain at least one match for the DAF-19 position weight matrix (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is supported by computational motif scanning of ChIP-seq peaks.

claim: X-boxes are preferentially found at central locations in FKH-8 ChIP-seq peaks.
source: Importantly, X-boxes are preferentially found also at central locations, suggesting they could be in close proximity to FKH-8-bound sites (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is supported by positional analysis of X-box motifs in ChIP-seq peaks.

claim: X-boxes are less significantly or not significantly enriched in ChIP-seq datasets for other FKH TFs.
source: X-boxes are less significantly or not significantly enriched in ChIP-seq datasets for other FKH TFs (Figure 2—figure supplement 2 and Figure 2—source data 2), which is consistent with specific co-binding of DAF-19 and FKH-8.
evidence: This is supported by comparative analysis of multiple FKH TF ChIP-seq datasets.

claim: Regulatory sequences for 34% of ciliome genes contain both X-box motifs and FKH-8 genomic binding.
source: Regulatory sequences for 34% of ciliome genes contain both X-box motifs and FKH-8 genomic binding (Figure 2F and Figure 2—source data 2).
evidence: This is based on integrated analysis of motif predictions and ChIP-seq data.

claim: The dual regulatory signature of X-box motifs and FKH-8 binding is present in 62% of core ciliome genes.
source: This dual regulatory signature is more prevalent in core ciliome genes (present in 62% of this gene category) than in subtype-specific ciliome (present in 6% of these genes) (Figure 2F and Figure 2—source data 2).
evidence: This is based on categorized analysis of ciliome genes.

claim: The dual regulatory signature of X-box motifs and FKH-8 binding is present in 6% of subtype-specific ciliome genes.
source: This dual regulatory signature is more prevalent in core ciliome genes (present in 62% of this gene category) than in subtype-specific ciliome (present in 6% of these genes) (Figure 2F and Figure 2—source data 2).
evidence: This is based on categorized analysis of ciliome genes.

claim: Most X-boxes are located less than 600 bp from the center of its closest FKH-8 ChIP-seq peak.
source: In addition, most X-boxes are located less than 600 bp from the center of its closest FKH-8 ChIP-seq peak (Figure 2G), this close proximity is a feature of core-ciliome components (found in 66% of core ciliome genes) but not for sub-type ciliome genes (only 9% of X-boxes found in this category contain a nearby FKH-8 peak) (Figure 2—figure supplement 2 and Figure 2—source data 2).
evidence: This is based on distance analysis between X-boxes and ChIP-seq peaks.

claim: 66% of core ciliome genes have X-boxes located less than 600 bp from a FKH-8 ChIP-seq peak.
source: In addition, most X-boxes are located less than 600 bp from the center of its closest FKH-8 ChIP-seq peak (Figure 2G), this close proximity is a feature of core-ciliome components (found in 66% of core ciliome genes) but not for sub-type ciliome genes (only 9% of X-boxes found in this category contain a nearby FKH-8 peak) (Figure 2—figure supplement 2 and Figure 2—source data 2).
evidence: This is based on categorized distance analysis.

claim: Only 9% of X-boxes in subtype ciliome genes contain a nearby FKH-8 peak.
source: In addition, most X-boxes are located less than 600 bp from the center of its closest FKH-8 ChIP-seq peak (Figure 2G), this close proximity is a feature of core-ciliome components (found in 66% of core ciliome genes) but not for sub-type ciliome genes (only 9% of X-boxes found in this category contain a nearby FKH-8 peak) (Figure 2—figure supplement 2 and Figure 2—source data 2).
evidence: This is based on categorized distance analysis.

claim: FKH-8 and DAF-19 interact bound to DNA.
source: Our results show that FKH-8 and DAF-19 interact bound to DNA (Figure 2—figure supplement 2 and ) and more importantly also in the nuclear soluble fraction free of chromatin (Figure 2H and Figure 2—source data 3).
evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation experiments using chromatin fractions.

claim: FKH-8 and DAF-19 interact in the nuclear soluble fraction free of chromatin.
source: Our results show that FKH-8 and DAF-19 interact bound to DNA (Figure 2—figure supplement 2 and ) and more importantly also in the nuclear soluble fraction free of chromatin (Figure 2H and Figure 2—source data 3).
evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation experiments using nuclear soluble fractions.

claim: FKH-8 and DAF-19 act together to regulate ciliome gene expression, particularly in core cilia components.
source: In summary, our data is consistent with FKH-8 and DAF-19 acting together to regulate ciliome gene expression, particularly in core cilia components.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on multiple lines of evidence including ChIP-seq, physical interaction, and mutant analysis.

claim: fkh-8(tm292) is a deletion downstream the FKH DNA binding domain.
source: The only available fkh-8 mutation, tm292, is a deletion downstream the FKH DNA binding domain, suggesting it might not be a null allele (Figure 2A, Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is based on molecular characterization of the tm292 allele.

claim: fkh-8(tm292) might not be a null allele.
source: The only available fkh-8 mutation, tm292, is a deletion downstream the FKH DNA binding domain, suggesting it might not be a null allele (Figure 2A, Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is inferred from the location of the deletion and supported by phenotypic comparison with the vlc43 deletion allele.

claim: fkh-8(vlc43) is a deletion allele that removes the whole fkh-8 coding region.
source: Thus, we built fkh-8(vlc43), a deletion allele that removes the whole fkh-8 coding region (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is based on the molecular design and characterization of the vlc43 allele.

claim: Both fkh-8 mutant alleles show significant expression defects in all reporters except for tub-1/Tub and the long peli-1/Peli1,2,3 and xbx-1 reporters.
source: Both fkh-8 mutant alleles show significant expression defects in all reporters except for tub-1/Tub and the long peli-1/Peli1,2,3 and xbx-1 reporters (Figure 3A and B Figure 3—figure supplement 1 and Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis of reporter expression in mutants.

claim: Lack of fluorescence reporter expression in fkh-8 mutants reflects enhancer activity defects and not the absence of the ciliated neurons per se.
source: Lack of fluorescence reporter expression in fkh-8 mutants reflects enhancer activity defects and not the absence of the ciliated neurons per se, as tub-1/Tub and the long peli-1/Peli1,2,3 reporters are expressed in 53 and 46 ciliated neurons respectively in fkh-8 mutants, similar to wild type expression levels (Figure 3—figure supplement 1 and Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by the observation that some reporters remain expressed in fkh-8 mutants, indicating neurons are present.

claim: Phenotypes are often more penetrant in fkh-8(vlc43) null allele than in the fkh-8(tm292).
source: Phenotypes are often more penetrant in fkh-8(vlc43) null allele than in the fkh-8(tm292) and both fkh-8(vlc43) and fkh-8(tm292) heterozygote animals show similar reporter expression levels as wild type indicating both alleles are recessive and tm292 is a hypomorph (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative comparison of phenotypes between the two alleles.

claim: Both fkh-8(vlc43) and fkh-8(tm292) heterozygote animals show similar reporter expression levels as wild type.
source: Phenotypes are often more penetrant in fkh-8(vlc43) null allele than in the fkh-8(tm292) and both fkh-8(vlc43) and fkh-8(tm292) heterozygote animals show similar reporter expression levels as wild type indicating both alleles are recessive and tm292 is a hypomorph (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of heterozygote animals.

claim: Both fkh-8 alleles are recessive.
source: Phenotypes are often more penetrant in fkh-8(vlc43) null allele than in the fkh-8(tm292) and both fkh-8(vlc43) and fkh-8(tm292) heterozygote animals show similar reporter expression levels as wild type indicating both alleles are recessive and tm292 is a hypomorph (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that heterozygotes show wild-type expression.

claim: fkh-8(tm292) is a hypomorph.
source: Phenotypes are often more penetrant in fkh-8(vlc43) null allele than in the fkh-8(tm292) and both fkh-8(vlc43) and fkh-8(tm292) heterozygote animals show similar reporter expression levels as wild type indicating both alleles are recessive and tm292 is a hypomorph (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that vlc43 shows stronger phenotypes than tm292.

claim: Endogenously tagged osm-5 shows panciliary expression in wild type animals.
source: Endogenously tagged osm-5 core cilome gene [osm-5(syb6528), osm-5::SL2::GFP::H2B] shows panciliary expression in wild type animals (Figure 3C), fluorescence intensity is greatly reduced in fkh-8(vlc43) animals (Figure 3C and D) further supporting the role of FKH-8 in direct control of ciliome gene expression.
evidence: This is supported by microscopy of the endogenously tagged strain.

claim: Fluorescence intensity of endogenously tagged osm-5 is greatly reduced in fkh-8(vlc43) animals.
source: Endogenously tagged osm-5 core cilome gene [osm-5(syb6528), osm-5::SL2::GFP::H2B] shows panciliary expression in wild type animals (Figure 3C), fluorescence intensity is greatly reduced in fkh-8(vlc43) animals (Figure 3C and D) further supporting the role of FKH-8 in direct control of ciliome gene expression.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative fluorescence intensity measurements.

claim: fkh-8(vlc43) animals show missing ift-20 expression in ten neurons including the four pairs of dopaminergic ciliated mechanosensory neurons.
source: fkh-8(vlc43) animals show missing ift-20 expression in ten neurons including the four pairs of dopaminergic ciliated mechanosensory neurons (CEPV, CEPD, ADE and PDE).
evidence: This is supported by reporter expression analysis in fkh-8 mutants.

claim: Expression of fkh-8 cDNA under the control of a dat-1 dopaminergic specific promoter in fkh-8(vlc43) animals is able to rescue ift-20 reporter expression.
source: Expression in fkh-8(vlc43) animals of fkh-8 cDNA under the control of a dat-1 dopaminergic specific promoter, which is unaffected in fkh-8 mutants (see below Figure 7 and Figure 7—source data 1), is able to rescue ift-20 reporter expression, consistent with a cell autonomously role of fkh-8 in the regulation of ciliome gene expression.
evidence: This is supported by rescue experiments.

claim: fkh-8 has a cell autonomous role in the regulation of ciliome gene expression.
source: Expression in fkh-8(vlc43) animals of fkh-8 cDNA under the control of a dat-1 dopaminergic specific promoter, which is unaffected in fkh-8 mutants (see below Figure 7 and Figure 7—source data 1), is able to rescue ift-20 reporter expression, consistent with a cell autonomously role of fkh-8 in the regulation of ciliome gene expression.
evidence: This is inferred from the ability of cell-type-specific expression to rescue the phenotype.

claim: Three independent transgenic lines with point mutations for FKH binding sites show broad expression defects both for ift-20 and xbx-1 reporters.
source: Three independent transgenic lines with point mutations for FKH binding sites show broad expression defects both for ift-20 and xbx-1 reporters (Figure 3—figure supplement 2 and Figure 3—source data 1 and 2).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of cis-regulatory mutant reporters.

claim: cis-mutation expression defects are stronger than the ones observed for fkh-8 mutant alleles.
source: cis-mutation expression defects are stronger than the ones observed for fkh-8 mutant alleles suggesting either other FKH factors can compensate the lack of fkh-8 or that cis-mutations could affect the binding of other TFs in addition to FKH-8.
evidence: This is based on comparison of phenotype severity between cis-mutants and trans-mutants.

claim: Other FKH factors might compensate for the lack of fkh-8.
source: cis-mutation expression defects are stronger than the ones observed for fkh-8 mutant alleles suggesting either other FKH factors can compensate the lack of fkh-8 or that cis-mutations could affect the binding of other TFs in addition to FKH-8.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the observation that cis-mutants are stronger than trans-mutants.

claim: cis-mutations could affect the binding of other TFs in addition to FKH-8.
source: cis-mutation expression defects are stronger than the ones observed for fkh-8 mutant alleles suggesting either other FKH factors can compensate the lack of fkh-8 or that cis-mutations could affect the binding of other TFs in addition to FKH-8.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the observation that cis-mutants are stronger than trans-mutants.

claim: FKH-8 binds five different locations in the daf-19 locus.
source: FKH-8 binds five different locations in the daf-19 locus (Figure 4A) while fkh-8 locus contains 3 putative X-box sites (Figure 2A), suggesting they could cross-regulate each other's expression.
evidence: This is based on ChIP-seq data analysis.

claim: fkh-8 locus contains 3 putative X-box sites.
source: FKH-8 binds five different locations in the daf-19 locus (Figure 4A) while fkh-8 locus contains 3 putative X-box sites (Figure 2A), suggesting they could cross-regulate each other's expression.
evidence: This is based on motif analysis of the fkh-8 locus.

claim: FKH-8 and DAF-19 could cross-regulate each other's expression.
source: FKH-8 binds five different locations in the daf-19 locus (Figure 4A) while fkh-8 locus contains 3 putative X-box sites (Figure 2A), suggesting they could cross-regulate each other's expression.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the presence of binding sites in each other's loci.

claim: daf-19d is specifically expressed in ciliated neurons.
source: Some of these isoforms are expressed in a mutually exclusive manner: daf-19d is specifically expressed in ciliated neurons while daf-19a/b isoforms are expressed in the rest of the nervous system but not in ciliated neurons (Senti et al., 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge about daf-19 isoform expression, supported by citation.

claim: daf-19a/b isoforms are expressed in the rest of the nervous system but not in ciliated neurons.
source: Some of these isoforms are expressed in a mutually exclusive manner: daf-19d is specifically expressed in ciliated neurons while daf-19a/b isoforms are expressed in the rest of the nervous system but not in ciliated neurons (Senti et al., 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge about daf-19 isoform expression, supported by citation.

claim: FKH-8 does not seem to be required for daf-19 expression in ciliated neurons.
source: Thus, our data suggest that, despite its extensive binding to daf-19 locus, FKH-8 does not seem to be required for daf-19 expression in ciliated neurons.
evidence: This is based on the observation that DAF-19::GFP expression is unaffected in fkh-8 mutants.

claim: Lack of all daf-19 isoforms derepresses fkh-8 in non-ciliated neurons.
source: In contrast to ciliated-neuron-specific expression pattern seen in wild type, FKH-8::GFP is expressed seemingly pan-neuronally in daf-19(m86); daf-12(sa204) double mutants (Figure 4B), suggesting a repressive role for DAF-19.
evidence: This is supported by observation of FKH-8::GFP expression in daf-19 mutants.

claim: DAF-19 has a repressive role on fkh-8 expression in non-ciliated neurons.
source: In contrast to ciliated-neuron-specific expression pattern seen in wild type, FKH-8::GFP is expressed seemingly pan-neuronally in daf-19(m86); daf-12(sa204) double mutants (Figure 4B), suggesting a repressive role for DAF-19.
evidence: This is inferred from the derepression of fkh-8 in daf-19 mutants.

claim: FKH-8::GFP expression in the PDE dopaminergic ciliated sensory neuron is unaffected in daf-19(m86); daf-12(sa204) double mutants.
source: FKH-8::GFP expression in the PDE dopaminergic ciliated sensory neuron is unaffected in daf-19(m86); daf-12(sa204) double mutants as assessed by co-localization with dat-1:cherry [91% PDE neurons are FKH-8::GFP positive in wild type animals and 92% in daf-19(m86); daf-12(sa204) mutants], suggesting that FKH-8::GFP expression is unaffected by the lack of daf-19 in ciliated neurons (Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative co-localization analysis.

claim: DAF-19D is not necessary for FKH-8 expression in ciliated neurons.
source: daf-19(m86) allele affects all isoforms; as DAF-19 isoform D is expressed in ciliated neurons, our results suggest DAF-19D is not necessary for FKH-8 expression in ciliated neurons.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that FKH-8 expression is maintained in ciliated neurons in daf-19(m86) mutants.

claim: DAF-19 isoforms A and B repress FKH-8 expression in non-ciliated neurons.
source: In contrast, DAF-19 isoforms A and B seem to repress FKH-8 expression in non-ciliated neurons, in agreement with this hypothesis, daf-19(of5), a mutant allele that specifically affects daf-19 a/b isoform expression (Figure 4A) shows similar pan-neuronal de-repression of FKH-8::GFP (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by the observation that daf-19(of5), which specifically affects A/B isoforms, shows similar derepression as the null allele.

claim: kap-1 ciliome gene reporter is de-repressed in daf-19(m86); daf-12(sa204) mutants.
source: Consistent with the role for DAF-19A/B as repressor (De Stasio et al., 2018; Senti et al., 2008), we also found kap-1 ciliome gene reporter is de-repressed in daf-19(m86); daf-12(sa204) mutants (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by reporter expression analysis in daf-19 mutants.

claim: kap-1 expression in ciliated neurons is independent of FKH-8.
source: Interestingly, both kap-1 expression in ciliated neurons as well as kap-1 de-repression in daf-19 mutants is independent of FKH-8 (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of kap-1 reporter in fkh-8 mutants.

claim: kap-1 de-repression in daf-19 mutants is independent of FKH-8.
source: Interestingly, both kap-1 expression in ciliated neurons as well as kap-1 de-repression in daf-19 mutants is independent of FKH-8 (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of kap-1 reporter in double mutants.

claim: DAF-19D induction is sufficient to produce ectopic ift-20 expression.
source: DAF-19D induction was sufficient to produce ectopic ift-20 expression while similar FKH-8 expression did not produce any significant effect (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by heat shock induction experiments.

claim: FKH-8 ectopic expression does not produce ectopic ift-20 expression.
source: DAF-19D induction was sufficient to produce ectopic ift-20 expression while similar FKH-8 expression did not produce any significant effect (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by heat shock induction experiments.

claim: RFX TFs display more instructive functions in ciliome gene expression than FKH-8.
source: These results, together with the stronger phenotypes of daf-19(m86) mutants, indicate that although both TFs are required for ciliome gene expression, RFX TFs display more instructive functions in ciliome gene expression.
evidence: This is inferred from the sufficiency experiments and comparison of mutant phenotypes.

claim: Loss of ift-20, peli-1, and xbx-1 reporter expression in triple mutants is greater than what will be expected for the multiplicative effect of the individual daf-19(m86); daf-12(sa204) and fkh-8(tm292); daf-12(sa204) phenotypes.
source: Loss of ift-20, peli-1, and xbx-1 reporter expression in triple mutants is greater than what will be expected for the multiplicative effect of the individual daf-19(m86); daf-12(sa204) and fkh-8(tm292); daf-12(sa204) phenotypes (Figure 4C and D and Figure 4—figure supplement 2) suggesting FKH-8 and DAF-19 could act synergistically.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis of reporter expression in double and triple mutants.

claim: FKH-8 and DAF-19 act synergistically.
source: Loss of ift-20, peli-1, and xbx-1 reporter expression in triple mutants is greater than what will be expected for the multiplicative effect of the individual daf-19(m86); daf-12(sa204) and fkh-8(tm292); daf-12(sa204) phenotypes (Figure 4C and D and Figure 4—figure supplement 2) suggesting FKH-8 and DAF-19 could act synergistically.
evidence: This is inferred from the greater than multiplicative effect in double mutants.

claim: osm-1 reporter expression in CEPV and CEPD neurons is unaffected or only slightly affected in fkh-8(tm292); daf-12(sa204) and daf-19(m86); daf-12(sa204) double mutants compared to daf-12(sa204) controls but is completely abolished in triple mutants.
source: We find osm-1 reporter expression in CEPV and CEPD neurons is unaffected or only slightly affected in fkh-8(tm292); daf-12(sa204) and daf-19(m86); daf-12(sa204) double mutants compared to daf-12(sa204) controls but is completely abolished in triple mutants (Figure 4E and Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by cell-specific reporter expression analysis.

claim: xbx-1 expression in PHA neurons is only significantly affected in triple mutants.
source: Similarly, xbx-1 expression in PHA neurons is only significantly affected in triple mutants (Figure 4E and Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by cell-specific reporter expression analysis.

claim: FKH-8 and DAF-19 act synergistically in the expression of specific ciliome genes and cellular contexts.
source: These data strongly suggest FKH-8 and DAF-19 act synergistically in the expression of specific ciliome genes and cellular contexts.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on cell-specific analysis of double and triple mutants.

claim: Mutations in several ciliome core components, including osm-5 and xbx-1, show cilium morphology defects.
source: Mutations in several ciliome core components, including osm-5 and xbx-1, whose reporters are affected in fkh-8 mutants, show cilium morphology defects (Blacque et al., 2004; Mukhopadhyay et al., 2007; Perkins et al., 1986; Starich et al., 1995).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Cilia length is controlled by a balance between cilia assembly and disassembly regulated by IFT.
source: In addition, cilia length is controlled by a balance between cilia assembly and disassembly regulated by IFT and mutants for ciliome components can produce both shortened or elongated cilia (Blacque et al., 2004; Burghoorn et al., 2007; Fujiwara et al., 1999).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Mutants for ciliome components can produce both shortened or elongated cilia.
source: In addition, cilia length is controlled by a balance between cilia assembly and disassembly regulated by IFT and mutants for ciliome components can produce both shortened or elongated cilia (Blacque et al., 2004; Burghoorn et al., 2007; Fujiwara et al., 1999).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: fkh-8(vlc43) animals show similar DiD staining compared to wild type.
source: Despite ciliome gene expression defects, fkh-8(vlc43) animals show similar DiD staining compared to wild type (Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by DiD staining assays.

claim: Cilium length in CEP and AWB neurons is significantly reduced in fkh-8(vlc43) mutants compared to controls.
source: Cilium length in CEP and AWB neurons is significantly reduced in fkh-8(vlc43) mutants compared to controls, while ADF neuron cilium length is significantly increased (Figure 5, Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative cilium length measurements.

claim: ADF neuron cilium length is significantly increased in fkh-8(vlc43) mutants.
source: Cilium length in CEP and AWB neurons is significantly reduced in fkh-8(vlc43) mutants compared to controls, while ADF neuron cilium length is significantly increased (Figure 5, Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative cilium length measurements.

claim: fkh-8 mutants display arborization defects in AWA cilia.
source: In addition, fkh-8 mutants display arborization defects in AWA cilia (Figure 5, Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis of AWA cilium arborization depth.

claim: osm-5 kinesin is required for correct AWB cilia morphology.
source: Of note, osm-5 kinesin, which our data show is a direct target for FKH-8, is required for correct AWB cilia morphology (Mukhopadhyay et al., 2007), which is also affected in fkh-8 mutants, suggesting both phenotypes could be correlated.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: AWB cilia morphology defects in fkh-8 mutants could be correlated with osm-5 being a direct target of FKH-8.
source: Of note, osm-5 kinesin, which our data show is a direct target for FKH-8, is required for correct AWB cilia morphology (Mukhopadhyay et al., 2007), which is also affected in fkh-8 mutants, suggesting both phenotypes could be correlated.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation connecting the molecular and phenotypic observations.

claim: fkh-8 mutants respond similarly to wild type animals to body gentle touch stimuli.
source: fkh-8 mutants respond similarly to wild type animals to body gentle touch stimuli, which are mediated by not ciliated neurons (Chalfie and Sulston, 1981; Figure 6—figure supplement 1), discarding general response or locomotory defects in fkh-8 mutants.
evidence: This is supported by gentle touch behavioral assays.

claim: Response to posterior harsh touch is unaffected in fkh-8(tm292) and fkh-8(vlc43) animals.
source: Response to posterior harsh touch, which is redundantly mediated by ciliated PDE and non-ciliated PVD neurons (Li et al., 2011) is also unaffected in fkh-8(tm292) and fkh-8(vlc43) animals, suggesting FKH-8 is not required to mediate this mechanosensory behavior (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by harsh touch behavioral assays.

claim: FKH-8 is not required to mediate posterior harsh touch response.
source: Response to posterior harsh touch, which is redundantly mediated by ciliated PDE and non-ciliated PVD neurons (Li et al., 2011) is also unaffected in fkh-8(tm292) and fkh-8(vlc43) animals, suggesting FKH-8 is not required to mediate this mechanosensory behavior (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of behavioral defects in fkh-8 mutants.

claim: No defects on basal slowing response are found in fkh-8(vlc43) null mutants.
source: No defects on basal slowing response are found in fkh-8(vlc43) null mutants, while both fkh-8 alleles are defective for nose touch responses (Figure 6A and B, Figure 6—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by basal slowing behavioral assays.

claim: Both fkh-8 alleles are defective for nose touch responses.
source: No defects on basal slowing response are found in fkh-8(vlc43) null mutants, while both fkh-8 alleles are defective for nose touch responses (Figure 6A and B, Figure 6—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by nose touch behavioral assays.

claim: fkh-8(vlc43) animals are slightly but significantly dauer constitutive at 27 °C compared to N2 controls.
source: fkh-8(vlc43) animals are slightly but significantly dauer constitutive at 27 °C compared to N2 controls (Figure 6C, Figure 6—source data 1), which might indicate fkh-8 mutants show defects in preventing dauer entry, a process mediated by ADF, ASI, and ASG ciliated neurons (Bargmann and Horvitz, 1991).
evidence: This is supported by dauer formation assays.

claim: Exposure to pheromones induces dauer entry in fkh-8(vlc43) animals less efficiently than in wild type animals.
source: Moreover, exposure to pheromones induces dauer entry in fkh-8(vlc43) animals less efficiently than in wild type animals [sixfold induction in wild type versus threefold induction in fkh-8(vlc43) animals; Figure 6C, Figure 6—source data 1], suggesting FKH-8 could also be required for correct dauer entry, which is mediated by ASJ ciliated neuron (Bargmann and Horvitz, 1991).
evidence: This is supported by pheromone-induced dauer formation assays.

claim: FKH-8 could be required for correct dauer entry.
source: Moreover, exposure to pheromones induces dauer entry in fkh-8(vlc43) animals less efficiently than in wild type animals [sixfold induction in wild type versus threefold induction in fkh-8(vlc43) animals; Figure 6C, Figure 6—source data 1], suggesting FKH-8 could also be required for correct dauer entry, which is mediated by ASJ ciliated neuron (Bargmann and Horvitz, 1991).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the reduced pheromone response.

claim: fkh-8(vlc43) null mutants show significant odor avoidance defects to 2-nonanone.
source: fkh-8(vlc43) null mutants, but not tm292 allele, show significant odor avoidance defects to 2-nonanone (AWB mediated) and defective odor attraction to 2-heptanone (mediated by AWC; Figure 6D and E, Figure 6—source data 1; Bargmann et al., 1993; Troemel et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by chemotaxis behavioral assays.

claim: fkh-8(vlc43) null mutants show defective odor attraction to 2-heptanone.
source: fkh-8(vlc43) null mutants, but not tm292 allele, show significant odor avoidance defects to 2-nonanone (AWB mediated) and defective odor attraction to 2-heptanone (mediated by AWC; Figure 6D and E, Figure 6—source data 1; Bargmann et al., 1993; Troemel et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by chemotaxis behavioral assays.

claim: fkh-8 mutants are attracted to NaCl similar to N2 controls.
source: fkh-8 mutants are attracted to NaCl similar to N2 controls, a response that is mediated mainly by ASE ciliated neurons (Bargmann and Horvitz, 1991; Figure 6G, Figure 6—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by NaCl chemotaxis assays.

claim: Avoidance response to SDS is significantly reduced both in fkh-8(vlc43) and fkh-8(tm292) animals.
source: In contrast, avoidance response to SDS, mediated by ASH and ASK ciliated neurons (Hilliard et al., 2002) and avoidance to copper, mediated by ASH, ASE, ADF and ADL ciliated neurons (Guo et al., 2015; Sambongi et al., 1999), were significantly reduced both in fkh-8(vlc43) and fkh-8(tm292) animals (Figure 6H,I, Figure 6—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by SDS avoidance assays.

claim: Avoidance to copper is significantly reduced both in fkh-8(vlc43) and fkh-8(tm292) animals.
source: In contrast, avoidance response to SDS, mediated by ASH and ASK ciliated neurons (Hilliard et al., 2002) and avoidance to copper, mediated by ASH, ASE, ADF and ADL ciliated neurons (Guo et al., 2015; Sambongi et al., 1999), were significantly reduced both in fkh-8(vlc43) and fkh-8(tm292) animals (Figure 6H,I, Figure 6—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by copper avoidance assays.

claim: FKH-8 is necessary for the correct response to a wide range of sensory stimuli (mechanical, gustatory or olfactory) that are mediated by different types of ciliated neurons.
source: In summary, our battery of behavioral assays reveals FKH-8 is necessary for the correct response to a wide range of sensory stimuli (mechanical, gustatory or olfactory) that are mediated by different types of ciliated neurons (ADF, ADL, ASE, ASG, ASH, ASI, ASJ, ASK, AWB, AWC, FLP, and OLQ).
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on multiple behavioral assays.

claim: Specific behaviors, such as attraction to NaCl or basal slowing response are sustained in fkh-8 mutants.
source: Some neurons controlling affected behaviors show corresponding morphological cilia defects in fkh-8 mutants, such as ADF, AWA, and AWB neurons. Nevertheless, we found that specific behaviors, such as attraction to NaCl or basal slowing response are sustained in fkh-8 mutants, suggesting retained sensory functions for particular neuron types, even with gene expression or morphological cilia defects (such as CEPs).
evidence: This is based on behavioral assay results.

claim: Particular neuron types retain sensory functions in fkh-8 mutants even with gene expression or morphological cilia defects.
source: Some neurons controlling affected behaviors show corresponding morphological cilia defects in fkh-8 mutants, such as ADF, AWA, and AWB neurons. Nevertheless, we found that specific behaviors, such as attraction to NaCl or basal slowing response are sustained in fkh-8 mutants, suggesting retained sensory functions for particular neuron types, even with gene expression or morphological cilia defects (such as CEPs).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that some behaviors are normal despite molecular and morphological defects.

claim: The establishment of specific orthology relationships between FKH members is challenging among distant species.
source: The establishment of specific orthology relationships between FKH members is challenging among distant species (Shimeld et al., 2010), precluding the direct assignment of the closest vertebrate ortholog for C. elegans FKH-8.
evidence: This is established knowledge about FKH family evolution, supported by citation.

claim: No vertebrate FKH TF has been shown to be involved in ciliogenesis in primary cilia cell types prior to this study.
source: To date, no vertebrate FKH TF has been shown to be involved in ciliogenesis in primary cilia cell types.
evidence: This reflects the state of knowledge in the field prior to the current study.

claim: In several vertebrate cell types that contain motile cilia, FoxJ1 FKH TF directly activates ciliome gene expression.
source: Nevertheless, in several vertebrate cell types that contain motile cilia, FoxJ1 FKH TF directly activates ciliome gene expression (Brody et al., 2000; Chen et al., 1998; Stubbs et al., 2008; Vij et al., 2012; Yu et al., 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: Mouse FOXJ1 can functionally substitute FKH-8 in C. elegans.
source: We find this to be the case as FoxJ1 cDNA expression under the dopaminergic promoter dat-1 rescues ift-20 expression similarly to fkh-8 cDNA (Figure 7A-C and Figure 7—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by rescue experiments.

claim: Mouse FoxN4 can functionally substitute FKH-8 in C. elegans.
source: We find FoxN4 expression also rescues ift-20 expression defects in fkh-8(vlc43) animals.
evidence: This is supported by rescue experiments.

claim: Mouse FoxI1 cannot functionally substitute FKH-8 in C. elegans.
source: Importantly, we find that conserved functionality is not observed for any vertebrate FKH TFs as expression of mouse FoxI1, a FKH TF involved in the development of several tissues but not reported to control cilia gene expression (Edlund et al., 2015), does not rescue fkh-8 mutant phenotype.
evidence: This is supported by rescue experiments.

claim: Specific FKH TFs might have the capacity to act as direct ciliome regulators, independently of being expressed in motile or sensory cilia cell types.
source: Altogether, this data suggests that specific FKH TFs might have the capacity to act as direct ciliome regulators, independently of being expressed in motile or sensory cilia cell types.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the functional conservation between FKH-8 and FOXJ1/FOXN4.

claim: Vertebrate sensory ciliogenesis is unaffected in FoxJ1 loss of function mutants.
source: Importantly, vertebrate sensory ciliogenesis is unaffected in FoxJ1 loss of function mutants (Choksi et al., 2014); thus, FoxJ1 role as a master regulator of ciliogenesis is restricted to motile ciliary cell types.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: FoxJ1 role as a master regulator of ciliogenesis is restricted to motile ciliary cell types.
source: Importantly, vertebrate sensory ciliogenesis is unaffected in FoxJ1 loss of function mutants (Choksi et al., 2014); thus, FoxJ1 role as a master regulator of ciliogenesis is restricted to motile ciliary cell types.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that sensory cilia are unaffected in FoxJ1 mutants.

claim: In C. elegans, FKH-2 is a downstream target of DAF-19 that controls expression of some ciliome components and cilium morphogenesis specifically in AWB neurons.
source: In C. elegans, another FKH TF, FKH-2, is a downstream target of DAF-19 that controls expression of some ciliome components and cilium morphogenesis specifically in AWB neurons (Mukhopadhyay et al., 2007).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: In Drosophila melanogaster, fd3F FKH transcription factor directly regulates expression of several ciliome genes in the chordotonal neurons.
source: Finally, in Drosophila melanogaster, fd3F FKH transcription factor directly regulates expression of several ciliome genes in the chordotonal neurons that contain atypical cilia with both sensory and motile functions (Newton et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: In Xenopus larval skin, FOXJ1 binding to ciliome gene promoters depends on the presence of RFX2.
source: Cooperativity between FKH and RFX has been reported in vertebrates, in motile multiciliated cells of Xenopus larval skin FOXJ1 binding to ciliome gene promoters depends on the presence of RFX2 (Quigley and Kintner, 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: In human airway multiciliated epithelial cell, RFX3 and FOXJ1 act synergistically in the activation of ciliome genes.
source: In addition, in human airway multiciliated epithelial cell, RFX3 and FOXJ1 act synergistically in the activation of ciliome genes (Didon et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Cooperative actions of DAF-19 and FKH-8 seem prevalent for core ciliome components.
source: Importantly, cooperative actions of DAF-19 and FKH-8 seem prevalent for core ciliome components while several sub-type specific ciliome genes are known targets for neuron-type-specific terminal selectors (Etchberger et al., 2007; Flames and Hobert, 2009; Zhang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is inferred from the enrichment of dual regulatory signatures in core ciliome genes.

claim: Several sub-type specific ciliome genes are known targets for neuron-type-specific terminal selectors.
source: Importantly, cooperative actions of DAF-19 and FKH-8 seem prevalent for core ciliome components while several sub-type specific ciliome genes are known targets for neuron-type-specific terminal selectors (Etchberger et al., 2007; Flames and Hobert, 2009; Zhang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: RFX role regulating ciliome expression predates the emergence of metazoans.
source: RFX role regulating ciliome expression predates the emergence of metazoans, where major cell type diversification has occurred (Chu et al., 2010; Piasecki et al., 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: FoxJ and FoxN constitute the most ancient FKH sub-families, present in choanoflagelate Monosiga brevicolis.
source: FoxJ and FoxN constitute the most ancient FKH sub-families, present in choanoflagelate Monosiga brevicolis, while FoxI subfamily is only present in bilaterians (Shimeld et al., 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge about FKH family evolution, supported by citation.

claim: FoxI subfamily is only present in bilaterians.
source: FoxJ and FoxN constitute the most ancient FKH sub-families, present in choanoflagelate Monosiga brevicolis, while FoxI subfamily is only present in bilaterians (Shimeld et al., 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge about FKH family evolution, supported by citation.

claim: The ability of RFX and FKH TFs to bind similar genomic regions is not limited to metazoans and is also present in fungi.
source: Moreover, the ability of RFX and FKH TFs to bind similar genomic regions is not limited to metazoans and it is also present in fungi.
evidence: This is supported by the example from S. pombe cited in the text.

claim: In Schizosaccharomyces pombe, Fkh2 FKH TF and Sak1 RFX TF bind the same regulatory regions to control cell cycle gene expression.
source: For example, in Schizosaccharomyces pombe, which lacks cilia and ciliome genes, Fkh2 FKH TF and Sak1 RFX TF bind the same regulatory regions to control cell cycle gene expression (Garg et al., 2015), suggesting that the joint actions for these TFs could be present before the split of fungi and metazoans.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: The joint actions of RFX and FKH TFs could be present before the split of fungi and metazoans.
source: For example, in Schizosaccharomyces pombe, which lacks cilia and ciliome genes, Fkh2 FKH TF and Sak1 RFX TF bind the same regulatory regions to control cell cycle gene expression (Garg et al., 2015), suggesting that the joint actions for these TFs could be present before the split of fungi and metazoans.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the observation in S. pombe.

claim: RFX and FKH TFs might have an inherent ability to cooperate that could explain convergent evolution of these TFs in ciliome regulation both in sensory and motile cilia cell types.
source: Alternatively, RFX and FKH TFs might have an inherent ability to cooperate that could explain convergent evolution of these TFs in ciliome regulation both in sensory and motile cilia cell types (Sorrells et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a speculative alternative hypothesis about the evolution of RFX/FKH cooperation.

claim: RFX and FKH role as co-regulators of ciliome gene expression could precede the emergence of cilia division of labor and the specialization of motile and sensory cilium in different cell types.
source: In light of these data, we hypothesize that RFX and FKH role as co-regulators of ciliome gene expression could precede the emergence of cilia division of labor and the specialization of motile and sensory cilium in different cell types (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is a speculative evolutionary hypothesis based on the data presented.

claim: In vertebrates, yet unidentified FKH TFs could act together with RFX in the regulation of ciliome gene expression in sensory ciliated cell types.
source: Regardless of the evolutionary history of events underlying RFX and FKH functions as direct regulators of ciliome gene expression, our results raise the possibility that, in vertebrates, yet unidentified FKH TFs could act together with RFX in the regulation of ciliome gene expression in sensory ciliated cell types (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is a speculative prediction based on the findings in C. elegans.

claim: FoxJ1 and FoxN4 mutants do not show major ciliome gene expression defects in non-motile ciliated cell types.
source: Importantly, although FoxJ1 and FoxN4 mutants do not show major ciliome gene expression defects in non-motile ciliated cell types (Brody et al., 2000; Campbell et al., 2016; Chen et al., 1998; Stubbs et al., 2008; Yu et al., 2008) a recent report describes ciliary defects in vertebrate Olfactory Sensory Neurons in Foxj1 mutants (Rayamajhi et al., 2023).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: A recent report describes ciliary defects in vertebrate Olfactory Sensory Neurons in Foxj1 mutants.
source: Importantly, although FoxJ1 and FoxN4 mutants do not show major ciliome gene expression defects in non-motile ciliated cell types (Brody et al., 2000; Campbell et al., 2016; Chen et al., 1998; Stubbs et al., 2008; Yu et al., 2008) a recent report describes ciliary defects in vertebrate Olfactory Sensory Neurons in Foxj1 mutants (Rayamajhi et al., 2023).
evidence: This is recent research supported by citation.

claim: Other members of FoxJ and FoxN subfamilies are broadly expressed in mouse neurons.
source: Other members of FoxJ and FoxN subfamilies are broadly expressed in mouse neurons, which all display primary cilia (Zeisel et al., 2018).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.
